title: The Boy Who Would Not Share the Sun
summary: Bram catches the warm morning sun in a glass jar so he can have its light and warmth all to himself, always. But the sun was meant to be shared, and as he hoards it, the whole valley grows cold and grey — and Bram must learn that some things are only warm when they are given away.

chapters.title: The Jar of Morning
chapters.body:
Bram was nine, and he loved the morning sun more than anything, and one day he found a way to keep it.

He lived in a narrow valley called Lowmeadow, where the sun came late and left early, slipping behind the high hills by mid-afternoon. And Bram loved that brief warm golden light so fiercely, and mourned its leaving so bitterly each day, that he had always wished he could somehow hold onto it. And then, on a market stall run by a strange old peddler, he found a jar — an ordinary-looking glass jar with a tight cork lid — and the peddler told him it was no ordinary jar.

"This jar catches light," the old peddler said. "Hold it open to the morning sun, and it will fill with the warmth and the glow, and when you cork it, the light stays — yours to keep, to open whenever you like, a piece of morning in a jar." The peddler's eyes glinted. "But I'll tell you what I tell everyone who buys it, boy, and most don't listen: the sun isn't yours to keep. It belongs to everyone. Catch a little, if you must. But don't be greedy with the light. Light hoarded goes strange."

Bram barely heard the warning. He bought the jar, and the next morning he ran out into the brief golden light and held the jar open to the rising sun, and watched it fill with warm glow like liquid gold, and corked it tight. And that afternoon, when the real sun had slipped behind the hills and Lowmeadow had gone grey and cold as it always did, Bram opened his jar in his room — and out spilled warm golden morning light, filling his room with sunshine and warmth, his own private piece of the sun.

It was wonderful. It was the most wonderful thing Bram had ever had. While the rest of the valley sat grey and chilly in the long afternoon shadow, Bram had summer in a jar, warmth and light whenever he wanted it, all to himself.

And that was exactly where the trouble began. Because Bram, having tasted what it was to keep the sun, wanted more of it. One jar's worth of morning ran out too fast. So he got more jars. Every morning, he ran out into the brief golden light and filled jar after jar after jar, corking the sunshine away, hoarding the warmth and the glow so he'd never be cold or grey again. He filled his room with jars of captured morning, and lived in private sunshine, and thought himself the cleverest and luckiest boy in the whole valley.

He did not notice, at first, that the more sun he caught and kept, the less there was for everyone else.

chapters.title: The Valley Grows Cold
chapters.body:
It came on slowly, the way these things do.

The mornings in Lowmeadow began to grow dimmer. The brief golden light that had always warmed the valley, however briefly, came weaker now, and greyer, and colder. At first no one understood why. The farmers muttered that the seasons were turning strange. The old folk said they couldn't remember a spring so grey and chill. The whole valley grew colder and darker, the crops struggling in the weak light, the people shivering through mornings that had once been golden.

But Bram knew why, though he tried not to think about it. It was the jars. Every morning he ran out and caught the sun — more and more of it, jar after jar — and every scrap of morning light he hoarded away in glass was a scrap of light that no longer fell on the valley. He was stealing the sun from Lowmeadow, a jar at a time, keeping for himself the warmth that was meant for everyone, and the valley was going cold and grey because its light was piling up, corked and hidden, in one greedy boy's room.

And here was the strange thing Bram noticed, the thing the peddler had warned him about: the hoarded light was going strange. The jars of captured morning that had glowed so warm and golden at first were dimming. The light in them, cut off from the sky, sealed away from the world, was slowly fading — growing pale, then wan, then grey, the warmth leaking out of it, until jar after jar held only a dull, cold, lifeless glow, like the memory of sunshine rather than the thing itself. The sun, it seemed, did not like to be kept. Caught and corked and hoarded, it withered, the way a cut flower withers in a vase — beautiful for a moment, then fading, because it had been taken from the thing that kept it alive.

Bram sat in his room full of jars, and the jars grew dimmer and colder around him, and outside the valley grew dimmer and colder too, and he began to understand the terrible bargain he'd made. He'd wanted to keep the sun's warmth for himself, always. But the sun's warmth couldn't be kept — it could only be hoarded, and hoarding killed it. The light he'd stolen from the valley was dying in its jars, giving him less and less warmth even as he caught more and more, while the valley he'd stolen it from grew colder and greyer and sadder by the day. He'd made everyone poorer, including himself. He was surrounded by jars of dying light, shivering in a cold grey room, in a cold grey valley, having taken the sun from everyone and found that it died the moment he kept it.

He went to find the old peddler, to ask how to undo it, and found the market stall, and the peddler still there, watching him with knowing eyes.

"The light's gone strange, has it?" the peddler said. "Dimming in the jars. And the valley gone cold. I did warn you, boy. The sun isn't yours to keep. It belongs to everyone — and here's the thing you didn't understand: it's only warm when it's shared. Light that falls on everyone stays golden and alive. Light hoarded by one goes grey and dies. That's the nature of it. You can't keep the sun. You can only kill it by trying."

"Then how do I fix it?" Bram asked, desperate, thinking of the cold grey valley and his room full of dying light.

"You know how," the peddler said simply. "You've known since I first warned you. The only question is whether you're willing to give back what you've hoarded — all of it — even though it means giving up your private sun."

chapters.title: The Light Given Back
chapters.body:
Bram carried all his jars of captured morning up to the top of the highest hill in Lowmeadow, where the grey light was weakest and the whole cold valley spread out below him, and he understood what he had to do, and how hard it would be.

He had to give the sun back. All of it. Every jar of hoarded light — even the ones still glowing, even his private sunshine, even the warmth he'd loved so fiercely and gathered so greedily. He had to uncork it all and let it go, release the stolen light back to the sky and the valley and everyone, and keep none of it for himself. And part of him didn't want to. Part of him thought: but if I give it all back, I'll have nothing. I'll be cold and grey like everyone else. Why should I give up my sun?

But he looked out over the cold grey valley — the shivering people, the struggling crops, the golden mornings he'd stolen and turned to grey — and he looked at his jars of dying, dimming light, giving him less warmth every day, and he understood the answer. He'd have nothing if he kept it too. That was the whole lesson. The hoarded sun was dying in its jars; keeping it gave him less and less; and it made everyone, including him, poorer and colder. There was no version where hoarding the sun made him warm. The only warmth left — the only way to have golden mornings again, for himself and everyone — was to give the light back, and let it be shared, and let it live.

So Bram, standing on the hilltop above the grey valley, began to uncork his jars.

He opened the first, and the pale hoarded light rose out of it — and the moment it was free, the moment it rejoined the sky and spread out over the valley instead of being sealed in glass, it brightened. The wan grey glow warmed back to gold as it spread, coming alive again the instant it was shared. Bram uncorked another jar, and another, faster now, releasing all the light he'd hoarded, and each jar's dying glow sprang back to golden life as it was freed and spread across the valley. He opened them all — every jar, all his private sunshine, everything he'd greedily gathered — and let all of it go, keeping none, giving the whole stolen sun back to the sky and the valley and everyone.

And the light, freed and shared, came fully alive. It spread golden across the whole valley of Lowmeadow, warm and bright and living, filling the grey cold mornings with sunshine again — richer and warmer than before, as all the hoarded light rejoined the world at once. The valley warmed. The people lifted their faces to the returning gold. The crops straightened in the strengthening light. And Bram stood on the hilltop with all his empty jars, having given away every scrap of the sun he'd tried to keep — and found that he was warmer, standing in the shared golden morning, than he had ever been in his room full of hoarded, dying light.

Because that was the thing the sun had taught him. Some things are only warm when they're shared. The sunlight that fell on everyone stayed golden and alive and warmed the whole valley, Bram included. The sunlight he'd hoarded for himself had gone grey and cold and dead, and made everyone poorer. He'd thought that keeping the sun meant having its warmth always. But the opposite was true: the only way to have the sun's warmth was to let it be everyone's, to share it freely, to never try to keep it. A jar of hoarded morning dies in the dark. But morning shared across a whole valley shines golden for all — and warms the one who shares it most of all.

Bram never caught the sun in a jar again. He gave the jars back to the old peddler, who took them with a knowing nod, and Bram went home through the golden, shared, living morning light of Lowmeadow, warm at last. And when the sun slipped behind the high hills that afternoon, as it always did, and the valley went into shadow, Bram did not mourn it or wish to keep it. Because he understood now that the sun would return the next morning, golden and warm, for everyone — and that its leaving each day was not a loss to be hoarded against, but simply the way of a thing that belongs to all and cannot be kept by one. He had learned to love the sun the only way it can truly be loved: with open hands, sharing it freely, and letting it go each evening knowing it would return each dawn — for him, and for everyone, warm and golden and alive, precisely because no one tried to keep it.
